cues.text: Let us turn now to Chapter 7, Organisational IP management.
So far we have looked at what intellectual property is and how it is protected.
Here the question changes: how does an organisation actually manage the intellectual property it owns and uses, day to day?
The source divides this into two approaches.
The first is proactive management.
This means acting before any dispute arises.
The source lists a set of practices.
First, maintain an IP inventory and a rights register, so the organisation knows what it owns and what rights attach to it.
Second, classify secrets, meaning decide which information is confidential and treat it accordingly.
Third, clear brands, which means checking that a brand can be used before relying on it.
Fourth, evaluate patents.
Fifth, document code provenance, that is, record where code came from.
Sixth, train staff, because people are often where IP problems begin.
Seventh, use reviewed contracts, so that agreements dealing with IP have been checked.
Eighth, run dependency and licence scans, and ninth, maintain a software bill of materials.
A software bill of materials is a list of the components, including third-party and open-source components, that make up a piece of software.
The source adds that the organisation should establish approval rules for three things: new dependencies, code reuse, and external contributions.
In other words, before someone adds a library, copies existing code, or accepts code from outside, there should be a defined route for approval.
The second approach is reactive management.
This handles problems after they arise.
The source names five elements: infringement evidence, negotiation, notices, litigation, and remediation.
So the organisation gathers evidence of infringement, may negotiate, may send or respond to notices, may go to litigation, and may need to remediate, meaning fix the problem.
Now the source gives a balance between the two.
Prevention is normally cheaper than disputes.
But the organisation should still reserve capacity for legitimate enforcement.
So prevention is the usual priority, yet the organisation must stay ready to enforce its rights when that is justified.
The source then gives an example workflow for managing a dependency, and the order matters.
Step one: identify the dependency and its version.
Step two: retrieve the licence.
Step three: determine the usage and distribution model, that is, how the software will be used and whether it will be distributed.
Step four: assess compatibility and obligations under the licence.
Step five: obtain approval.
Step six: preserve notices and source offers where required.
Step seven: monitor changes, because versions and licences can change over time.
Two cautions follow.
First, a licence scan is a starting point, not a legal conclusion.
A scan tool can flag what needs attention, but it does not settle what the licence legally requires.
Second, there are options when a problem is found.
Commercial licensing is an alternative if the rights holder offers it.
And replacing incompatible code can be appropriate.
Finally, the source widens the view to global issues.
These include unequal access to software, the costs of registration and enforcement, and piracy.
The source says we should respect creators while also considering accessibility, open standards, education, local innovation, and fair competition.
The closing point sums up the tension: IP can be both an incentive and a barrier.
It rewards and encourages creation, yet it can also limit access, particularly where cost and resources are unequal.
Good organisational management keeps both sides of that in view.
